module_title: Basic Structure of an Atom and Subatomic Particles
introduction: An atom is the smallest unit of ordinary matter that forms a chemical element. Every solid, liquid, gas, and plasma is composed of neutral or ionized atoms. They are incredibly small, but they are made up of even smaller components.

core_concepts.title: Subatomic Particles
core_concepts.description:
1. Electron ($e^-$): Negatively charged (-), has negligible mass. Orbits the nucleus. 
2. Proton ($p^+$): Positively charged (+), mass is roughly 1836 times that of an electron. Resides inside the nucleus. 
3. Neutron ($n^0$): Neutral (no charge), mass is almost equal to a proton. Also resides inside the nucleus.

core_concepts.title: The Nucleus
core_concepts.description:
Discovered by: Ernest Rutherford (via the Gold Foil Experiment). 
It is the dense, central core of the atom where protons and neutrons reside (collectively called 'Nucleons'). Almost the entire mass (weight) of an atom is concentrated in its nucleus.

core_concepts.title: Atomic Number (Z)
core_concepts.description:
The 'Number of Protons' present in the nucleus of an atom. 
Formula: $Z = p$ (In a neutral atom, $Z = p = e$). 
Example: Carbon has 6 protons, so its atomic number is 6.

core_concepts.title: Mass Number (A)
core_concepts.description:
The total sum of protons and neutrons present in the nucleus. 
Formula: $A = p + n$ 
Example: Sodium has 11 protons and 12 neutrons, so its mass number is $A = 11 + 12 = 23$.

important_entities.name: The Missing Neutron
important_entities.significance: Hydrogen (specifically the isotope Protium - $^1_1H$) is the ONLY element in the entire periodic table that has 'zero neutrons' in its nucleus. It consists of just 1 proton and 1 electron.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Exam Trap: 'What is the fundamental property that identifies an element?' Students often choose Atomic Mass. FALSE! The true identity of an element is its 'Atomic Number' (number of protons). If neutrons change, it's an isotope. If electrons change, it's an ion. But if protons change, it becomes a completely different element.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: An element is written as $_Z^AX$ (where A is on top and Z is on the bottom). To find the number of neutrons ($n$), simply subtract the bottom number from the top number ($n = A - Z$).

exam_strategy_tips: A direct Railway/SSC question: 'What is the size of an atomic nucleus?' Answer: $10^{-15}$ meters (1 Fermi), whereas the size of the whole atom is much larger at $10^{-10}$ meters (1 Angstrom).
